questions.explanation: The categories are best understood as answers to the question of what the party is trying to convert the intrusion into, because that determines almost everything else about the operation. A state-aligned group is usually working toward a strategic picture of another state's capabilities, which is why its operations are patient, its footholds are low-noise, and it is often content to watch for long periods without touching anything. A criminal group is running a business: it buys access cheaply, reaches as many victims as the tooling allows, and monetises through resale, fraud or extortion, so its priorities are reliability, scale and cost per victim, and it will abandon an unprofitable line quickly. An activist group wants the story to travel, so amplification is part of the operation rather than a side effect, and publishing something inconsequential is entirely consistent with that. An insider is the odd one out, because the objective is often not the point at all: what an insider has that an outsider does not is legitimate access plus knowledge of where the value sits, so the analysis has to start from what their role already permits. The value of the categories is that each one implies a different detection profile, a different containment cost and a different disclosure decision, which is why treating them as interchangeable produces controls that suit one of them and miss the rest.
questions.hint: Ask what each party wants to end up with, and for the insider ask what their role already gives them.

questions.explanation: Dwell time is one of the most informative fields in a compromise, and the reason is that it is expensive for both sides. An adversary that stays for a year is accepting a year of exposure to patching, log review, credential rotation and re-baselining, and is also accepting that its own infrastructure ages and its access degrades. Nobody pays that cost unless the return is spread over the same period, which points at an objective that accrues slowly: understanding what is reachable from where, learning the shape of the estate and its trust relationships, waiting for the right moment or the right person. Choosing not to escalate is therefore evidence, not indecision, and the absence of privilege is better read as an adversary being careful about detection than as an adversary having failed. The second option makes the mistake of reading a compromise only in terms of access obtained rather than knowledge gained, and knowledge is frequently the product: an actor with a foothold in a low-value system learns the addressing, the naming, the accounts of interest and the paths between systems, all of which is durable and none of which requires privilege. The third reverses the causality, since a deliberate operator who escalated immediately would be announcing themselves, and the whole value of the position is that it can be used later. The fourth is the ordinary interpretation of leftover artefacts and it is worth resisting, because tooling is often left deliberately as a tripwire or as a way back, and its presence says little about whether the operator is still there.
questions.hint: Ask what an adversary gives up by staying, and what that cost is worth.

questions.explanation: The presence of a price is the strongest single clue in this list, because it tells you the operation has a unit economics problem to solve. Someone is paying per victim, which means the group is optimising cost against yield, which means the behaviours that fall out of that are predictable: a foothold that can be reused is reused, tooling that works once is not rebuilt, and the group will spend effort on the steps that raise the conversion rate rather than the ones that make the entry more elegant. The two things that follow from this and matter most for defence are that the same indicators recur across unrelated victims, which is what makes a shared blocklist worth having, and that the group abandons anything unprofitable quickly, which means a change of tooling after a public write-up is evidence of the business responding rather than of a different group. The second option reads a business model as an ideology, and the fact that the victims are unrelated organisations is actively evidence against a single cause, since a cause-bound group picks targets. The third reads a commercial measurement as state accounting, and the two have incompatible requirements: a state programme can sustain a long unprofitable operation, which is exactly the property the pricing excludes. The fourth mistakes efficiency for sloppiness, and the judgement is backwards, because the entry point is the part of the chain most worth protecting and a professional group treats it accordingly.

questions.explanation: When the objective is attention, the record that matters is not the record that damages but the record that is seen. That changes what gets included, and it is the source of the two things that make activist leaks awkward to handle: a much larger volume than a targeted operation would produce, and a much weaker signal per item. Publishing an inconsequential record alongside forty consequential ones costs nothing, because nobody reads the small ones and the ones that do read them are exactly the audience the operation wants. It also means that volume is not evidence of severity, which is the trap for anyone assessing the impact of a disclosure. The second option applies an evidentiary standard that belongs to a different kind of claim, and it does misjudge how these things actually land: a claim is usually accepted or rejected as a whole, and one weak item is not what defeats it. The third is the same mistake pointed at a different audience, and it inverts the direction of causation, because the volume is a feature chosen for effect rather than a requirement imposed by an adjudicator. The fourth is a genuinely sharp observation about a different question, since proving access does sometimes rest on a single artefact, but that reasoning does not explain publishing the rest: a small demonstrated access would have been the cheaper and more credible move, and an operation optimising for reach has no reason to prefer it.

questions.explanation: The defining property of an insider is that every access they exercise is legitimate, which is exactly what makes the case hard. There is no failed sign-in to alert on, no account to block, no address to deny, and no boundary being crossed, because they are already inside it and always have been. The exposure is therefore a function of what the role can reach rather than of any attempt to reach it, and the useful controls follow from that: narrow what the role can reach, so that the amount available to copy is small; make access narrow in time as well as in scope, so that the data is only reachable when the work requires it; and notice use that is out of character for the role, whether by volume, by timing or by which of the available data is being touched. Volume and pattern are the reliable signals here and intent is not, which is why the framing matters. The second option is the instinct to protect the control rather than the access, and it is a real weakness in some designs but it is not the asymmetry in question, since knowing where a control is written down does not grant the data. The third and the fourth both look for a special circumstance to attach the suspicion to, and both will miss the ordinary case, which is the case that matters: a person doing their job, with their own credentials, at their own desk, for hours at a time.
questions.hint: Ask what is different about their access, and which part of it a control can actually bound.

questions.explanation: A supply-chain compromise is defined by the fact that it does not have to defeat anything. It is signed by the publisher, it is fetched from the address the consumer already trusts, it passes the same checks as any other update, and it is executed in a position that usually has more privilege and more reach than the person who introduced it. Every control the consumer has is doing exactly what it was designed to do and returning the correct answer, because from its point of view the artefact is genuine. This is why the reach is not a function of how many organisations were targeted but of how many consume the dependency, and why the fix cannot be a scanning control aimed at known bad artefacts: the artefacts were not bad at the point of detection. The defences that do work are about reducing the blast radius and about making provenance carry more information, such as building from a source that can be inspected, signing not just the artefact but the build that produced it, and limiting what the component is permitted to do at runtime. The second and fourth options each explain the reach by something other than trust, and both are true of the situation in a trivial sense while explaining nothing: a large install base and a familiar channel are how the thing travels, not why it succeeds. The third is the one that is sometimes true and is the most useful of the three, because a genuine gap in signing hygiene is a specific and fixable cause, but it is a cause of one campaign rather than a description of the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what every control along the way was asked to check, and what the correct answer was.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a supply-chain compromise inherits trust rather than having to earn it

options.text: It came in through the front of the trust system, so it inherited the trust of every build and every downstream consumer that verified the signature and ran the ordinary steps

options.misconception: explains the reach by scale alone
options.text: It was installed on more machines than the publisher had, so the number of affected systems exceeded anything the publisher could reasonably have declared

options.misconception: explains the reach by a signing window
options.text: It was published during a window in which the signing key had not been rotated, so every consumer that fetched it in that window accepted it without checking anything

options.misconception: explains the reach by the delivery channel
options.text: It arrived over the same channel as the ordinary updates, so consumers had no way to see that it came from a different source even if they had looked

questions.explanation: A watering-hole attack works because it targets a place the victim has already decided to trust, and there are two independent trust decisions involved, which is why the position is stronger than it first appears. The network has already granted permission for staff to reach that address, so any rule about which destinations may be contacted is already permitting it and the request is not unusual. The browser has already established that this origin is safe, so content from it is not treated as suspicious, and the origin is a legitimate one to run code in. An attacker in that position therefore inherits two allowances that were granted for an unrelated reason, and neither has to be broken. The second option is a genuine and useful property of having a valid certificate, but it does not do what the option claims: a valid certificate stops a warning, it does not remove the checks that decide whether content is allowed to run, and it says nothing about the outbound request the script makes. The third confuses a position that can observe its own visitors with a position on the path between two parties, and a page cannot read what is typed into other sites. The fourth is the belief that makes this technique interesting, and it is also wrong for a reason worth being precise about: reaching an internal address from inside the network is possible from the compromised site's visitors' browsers in some configurations, but that is a consequence to be tested rather than an assumption to be relied on, and it is not the same as the attacker holding a foothold.
questions.hint: Ask what the staff's network and the staff's browser have both already decided about that address.

questions.explanation: The dilemma is a genuine one and there is no position that is right in general, which is why reasonable people with the same information reach different conclusions. Publishing converts a private capability into a public one, and the effect on defenders depends on how fast the ecosystem patches, how fast organisations deploy, and how many people read the disclosure, while the effect on attackers is immediate and reliable. Withholding it leaves the capability private, which is better for defence against that particular actor and worse for everyone else, and it converts the problem into a negotiation in which the finder has no leverage beyond the credibility of the demonstration and no assurance that anything will happen. Both sides of that trade are the same trade, which is why the practical answer has moved towards a middle path: a private channel, a stated deadline, and a promise to publish if the deadline passes, so the withholding is conditional and the pressure is public. The second option gets the exposure backwards, because the interest of every jurisdiction with a disclosure regime is precisely to make the safer option viable, and a finder who reports in good faith is not in the position this describes. The third and the fourth are both real concerns that have been handled badly in individual cases, and neither is the structural tension. The dilemma is about who bears risk and who has control, not about legal or personal safety.
questions.hint: Ask who gains and who loses in each of the two options, and who has control in each.

questions.explanation: The risk window is the interval between the flaw being usable and the fix being present in the system that an attacker would actually reach, and in a chain that interval is set by the slowest step rather than by the one that is easiest to fix. A library patch on a Tuesday changes nothing for anyone until the product that embeds it ships a build containing it, and the earliest any customer can install is the earliest that build exists. The quarterly cadence then extends it again, and neither party is at fault in the way the argument usually goes: the library maintainer cannot ship a patch into releases that do not exist yet, and the product team cannot ship a build for a fix that has not been published. That is why the useful response is not to assign blame but to change the chain: know the components you depend on and how far behind you are on each, so the exposure can be stated in advance rather than reconstructed afterwards, and have a stated position on what you do when a component has a serious flaw and no release is due for months. The second option stops the clock at the moment that is easiest to control and is the framing that makes the maintainer's remediation look complete. The third concentrates blame on the party nearest the end, which produces good compliance pressure and no change in the interval. The fourth measures in units chosen for reporting convenience rather than for risk.
questions.hint: Ask the earliest date a fix could be present in the system an attacker would reach.

questions.explanation: The word coordinated is doing all the work in this exchange, and it is worth being precise about what makes a process coordinated rather than merely private. Coordination means the two sides have agreed on a sequence: the finder reports privately, the vendor acknowledges within a stated period, works to a stated target, and if the target passes without a fix the finder publishes. The channel and the deadline are what make that agreement real, because without them there is nothing to be coordinated with. A vendor that accepts reports and promises nothing has not adopted coordinated disclosure; it has adopted a channel through which to receive information without any obligation attaching to it, and the finder is left holding a capability and a secret with no way to move either. The second option mistakes a practice for a commercial arrangement, and the fee question is a separate matter that a disclosure policy can address on its own terms. The third is a real observation about estimation and it is not a reason against deadlines, because every workable process uses a default period rather than a promise, so the objection is answered by having a default rather than abandoned. The fourth has the sequence exactly backwards, and the reason it is a common belief is that a finding of a public post is often what forces a vendor's hand; the resolution is a promised deadline, not a promise to publish first.
questions.hint: Ask what the finder gets in exchange for withholding publication, and what enforces it.

questions.explanation: A scope list is a statement about what can be demonstrated, and reading it as a statement about what is dangerous is the most common misreading. A scope exists so that a report has a defined object and a defined way of being true about that object. Social engineering requires persuading a real person, which cannot be shown by a write-up and would require the company to hand its own staff over to a social engineering exercise. Physical entry requires being on site, which a remote programme has no way to supervise and no basis to verify. Another customer's system is outside anything the finder may touch, and asking for a report about it asks the company to investigate a breach of a different party. A retired version is excluded because a fix cannot be delivered into it, so a finding there is real but unactionable, and rewarding it would be paying for a note in a drawer. The second option is what a reader assumes, and it is why exclusion lists produce so much argument, but the practical effect is identical either way and the demonstration criterion is the one that decides what to do with an incoming report. The third confuses the exclusions with a severity policy, and note that a physical entry report may be far more serious than the software findings being paid for. The fourth invents a redirection the programme does not provide.
questions.hint: Ask what a finder would have to do to show each of these, and who would have to cooperate.

questions.explanation: A kit is designed to be repeatable, and repeatability comes from removing the parts of the operation that need skill or judgement. Everything variable is either a domain name or a piece of branding, so the marginal cost of the thousandth target is a text substitution, which is exactly the economics that make phishing a business rather than a craft. Any control that depends on the page being distinguishable is therefore fighting an adversary with a cost structure that favours them: the kit changes, the rule does not, and the rule is written once. The control that wins is the one that changes what the stolen item is worth. If a captured password is not sufficient to authenticate, then the harvest produced nothing an operator can use, whatever the page looked like and wherever it was hosted, and the entire kit becomes worthless without anyone having to recognise it. That is a property of the credential rather than of the delivery. The second is a real control that is worth having and it is also a race that the kit's operator can lose gracefully by moving hosts, and concentrated hosting is an economic choice rather than a technical limit. The third is the control most programmes actually rely on and its weakness is the one the kit is built to exploit. The fourth is the most seductive and the most dangerous of the four, because the factor is fetched by the same browser on the same page, so a kit that asks for both gets both.
questions.hint: Ask what the operator has after a successful harvest, and which control changes that.

questions.explanation: Credential stuffing is a volume attack with a very specific shape: a very large set of pairs, each tried exactly once against many accounts, with the operator willing to be slow because the pairs are free. Slow is the part that makes it awkward, because every control designed against a flood is calibrated to volume, and an operator who stays under the threshold has defeated the calibration. What makes it work is that the pairs came from somewhere else, so what has to be limited is how many guesses a single account absorbs rather than how many arrive from one place. Counting per account means the relevant limit is the same for every source, a distributed attempt and a single-source attempt hit the same wall, and the account that is being tried repeatedly is the one that gets protected. Counting per source is the failure mode: it treats a botnet as many attackers and an attacker with many addresses as many legitimate users. The second is the same error one layer up, since an operator who is being blocked rotates, and the hosting provider is not a party with any interest in reporting the traffic. The third is attractive and, as stated, impossible: a service learns of a breach after the fact, at best from a public dump, and the useful work is done long before that. The fourth is a guess about the adversary's tooling, and interactive challenges have been solved mechanically for years; the property that actually holds is the one in the first option, namely that the credential is not the whole of authentication.
questions.hint: Ask what the operator is optimising, and therefore which unit a limit should be counted in.

questions.explanation: Every token in this design is a bearer token, and a bearer token has exactly one requirement: whoever presents it is the session. There is no second condition, so possession is sufficient, and the set of ways to obtain one is the whole of the attack surface. Stolen means copied from a log, from a proxy, from a backup, from a shared machine, from a referrer, or from a browser that stored it somewhere accessible, and none of those require any interaction with the service. Binding adds the missing condition by requiring something at presentation that the token itself does not carry: a key that lives in the client, a device the service can identify, or a channel property the service can check. The thief who copied the token does not have that, so a valid token presented from the wrong place is refused. Notice what this does and does not solve. It does nothing about the attacker who has compromised the client itself, because then they have the key too, and it does nothing to stop a legitimate user from being tricked into acting on a session that is genuinely theirs. The second and third options are both real techniques and both are about time, which is the wrong axis, because a stolen token is used within seconds in practice and both techniques leave a window in which it works. The fourth is a category error that is very common: a signature protects the token against modification, and a hijack does not modify the token, it presents an unmodified one.

Once a channel is protected against a passive observer, what remains is the question of who is at the other end, and an active party answers that question by being the other end. The check that closes this is one that compares what is presented against an expectation the client already holds: a chain that ends in a key in the client's trust store, or a key the client has pinned, or a fingerprint configured out of band. Any of these makes a substituted endpoint fail the comparison, and the failure is visible before anything of value is sent. The second option is the most widespread belief and it is the one that produces the worst surprise, because protection against reading is exactly what a well-configured connection provides and it says nothing about whether the far end is who it claims to be; that is why an encrypted connection to a substituted endpoint is worse than no encryption, since it removes the user's ability to notice by eye. questions.explanation: A query has a name in it, and the intuitive behaviour is to answer that name and nothing else. The behaviour this attack needs is the opposite: the resolver takes records for other names out of the same reply and stores them as though it had been asked. The weakness is that the check is often not made, so a reply to a query about a name the attacker controls can carry records for any name at all. questions.explanation: Two parsers reading the same bytes is a problem only when they can disagree about the meaning of those bytes, and here they disagree about the one thing that determines what the bytes are: where the current request ends. There are more than one way to say that, and a request that is well formed under one reading and contains two requests under the other is not malformed, it is ambiguous, and the two components resolve it differently. The front end sees one request, applies its rules to it, and forwards what it believes it checked. The service behind reads a different boundary and finds a second request inside, one that the front end never saw and never authorised. The result is a request that arrives at a protected service without having passed the protection, and it inherits whatever authority the front end's own connection carries, which is why the interesting cases are internal destinations. The analytical consequence is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly: a plant is designed to be convincing, so the presence of a strong indicator is not confirmation of origin, it is confirmation that the adversary wanted it considered, and that consideration is itself worth understanding. The correct posture is to hold several hypotheses at once, to ask for each one which artefacts it explains, and to prefer the hypothesis that accounts for the whole set over the one that accounts for most of it and treats the remainder as noise. A second consideration is which artefacts are harder to plant. Something in the adversary's own infrastructure is more credible than something left in a location the adversary chose to stage, and something that would only exist as a by-product of the intrusion is harder to fake than something deliberately deposited. The second and third options both collapse the ambiguity by assumption, and they are the two conclusions the evidence has been arranged to encourage. questions.explanation: A sinkhole converts a name into an observation point, and what comes back is whatever the clients that use that name send to it. For a name being used to reach a command service, that is close to a list of the infected machines, with the timing of each contact, which is a genuinely useful set of facts and the reason defenders do this. It is a list, though, and the list has boundaries. Machines that were reconfigured to use a different name before the redirection are not in it, and a party who notices that their traffic is going somewhere that answers oddly will change the mechanism, at which point the sinkhole is a record of a channel that no longer exists. A sinkhole also does not tell the observer anything about those machines, because it sees a request and not the host that made it, unless something in the request or the path identifies it, and it says nothing about what the clients already have, which is the question an investigation usually needs answered. The second option mistakes a sighting for an identification and then assumes the identification extends to everything the machine does. The third confuses the direction of the change, since the redirection is for the observer's own use and reveals nothing about the name that was replaced. The fourth is an assumption about the infected machines that contradicts the reason a sinkhole works, which is that they are using the name as instructed.

questions.explanation: The two designs are easy to confuse and the difference between them is the whole content of the decision. A sinkhole that answers with a page of the observer's choosing keeps the client's connection working, which means a legitimate user of the name sees something wrong and a legitimate service that used the name keeps functioning in a degraded way, and the observer keeps the channel available to study. A sinkhole that returns an address which does not answer takes the connection down, and that is the stronger action: it removes the channel, and it also removes the name from use for everyone else. questions.explanation: There are two distinct things a redirection of this kind can be for, and they pull in opposite directions on the same infrastructure. One is observation: the channel is kept reachable so that the party continues to use it and the traffic can be studied, and the value is in what the traffic reveals. The other is removal: the channel is made unreachable so the party cannot use it, and the value is that a set of machines stops receiving instructions. A sinkhole that answers is doing the first, and a sinkhole that returns nothing is doing the second, and it is quite possible to run one that is nominally the second while paying the cost of the first. Once the clients have moved to another name, the removal is complete and the observation has also ended, and the remaining cost is the effort of watching an obsolete channel. That is the state described here and it is worth recognising because it is easy to leave in place: the infrastructure is running, the alerts are quiet, and nobody has asked what the channel is now for. The second option invents a protective effect from continued contact, which is the opposite of the case, since a machine that is still talking has not switched and is still under the other party's control. The third reduces the value to a count, and a count of a set that is shrinking is not a control. The fourth is the belief that makes the operation look justified regardless, and it is only true while the name is the only route.

questions.explanation: Resilience in this setting is a design property and it comes from one decision more than any other: keeping the channel out of the same place as everything else. An operator who hosts the command channel on infrastructure that is also doing ordinary work, or who registers the name through arrangements that are not tied to the operation, loses the channel at a cost measured in time and money rather than in access. That is a very different failure from losing a foothold, which is where the intrusion is and which the operator would have to rebuild from scratch. It is also why the domain being pursued is not the interesting part: taking a name is slow, contested and reversible, since a new name can be registered and the clients pointed at it. The second option is a real property of infrequent contact and it is not what the description turns on, since a channel contacted rarely is also one that has fewer opportunities to be seen, but the timing is a minor contributor compared to the separation. The third inverts the causality, treating pressure as evidence of the operator losing when it is evidence of the defender having found something. The fourth is a genuine capability and a partial answer, since a name can be moved, but it says nothing about the operator's position and it is the least important of the three.

questions.explanation: Randomising the interval attacks a specific detection technique and nothing more. Rules of this kind work by finding regularity: a period that repeats to within a small tolerance is a strong signal, and a host that contacts the same external address every sixty seconds is not common enough to be mistaken for a person checking something. Spreading the contacts removes that regularity, so the cheapest class of rule stops matching, and that is a real gain. Everything else about the contact is unchanged, and it has to be, because the implant still needs to reach the controller. The contact still happens, so anything watching for outbound connections sees it; the volume is still small but still there, and it still goes to the same place, so a rule about the destination still matches. The most reliable detection against a beacon of this kind is not about timing at all, it is about the relationship between the host and the destination and the fact that the relationship is one the host has no reason to have. The second and third both claim more than the change delivers, since a delay changes when a packet leaves and not where it comes from, and a length change does not defeat a rule keyed on destination and periodicity. questions.explanation: The right control for each campaign depends on what the campaign actually needs from the defender, and the one that depends least on recognition is the one worth having. Campaign B needs a correct pair, and the two controls that remove its value are a per-account limit and a second factor, because together they mean a stolen pair is not a usable credential and a given account can absorb only a bounded number of attempts regardless of how many sources are used. Neither depends on noticing the traffic, which is what makes the answer robust. The other three each depend on recognising something, and that is the reason the mapping in the distractors is attractive and wrong. A page that reuses a layout across a hundred targets is a real pattern, but a control keyed on it is keyed on the attacker's current infrastructure, and reusing infrastructure is exactly the thing a kit's operator gives up when it costs them the campaign. A request whose identifier changed is stopped by asking whether the signature covered that identifier, which is a property of how the signature is computed rather than a control applied to traffic. A trusted name is a genuine and hard problem, and restricting destinations and origins is a mitigation of value rather than a defeat.
questions.hint: Ask what each campaign needs from the defender, and which answer does not depend on being recognised.
questions.learningObjective: match a campaign to the control that actually stops it

answer.exemplar: The reason attribution stops short of certainty is a structural one rather than a limitation of effort, and it is worth stating because it changes what a good assessment looks like. The artefacts available are the adversary's: the tools they chose, the defaults they left, the hours they worked, the mistakes they made, the things they took care to avoid. Some of those are choices, and a choice can be informative because it costs something to make. Most are not, and a default output of a widely available tool is produced by every party who has not changed the setting, so it has a high rate of innocent production and carries almost no information about who made it. Even the informative ones point at a group rather than at an operation, because tools and habits are shared and outlive the campaigns that used them, so the link from an artefact to an organisation is made by the analyst rather than read off the evidence. That is why a defensible assessment does not name a source; it states a graded claim, names the observations the claim rests on, says which of them are distinctive and which are not, and says what observation would move it. The value of this form is that it survives contact with the next piece of evidence. An assessment that named a source has nothing to do when a contradicting artefact appears except be withdrawn, which is what makes false flags effective, and an assessment that named a probability has a prediction to check. It also names what is being claimed, and the distinction matters because the two claims are routinely confused: who the party probably is, and what they were trying to achieve. The second is usually better evidenced than the first, it is more directly useful, and an assessment that separates the two is more useful than one that resolves them into a single confident sentence.

questions.explanation: Most artefacts are defaults that anyone produces, and the informative ones point at a group rather than an operation, so the link to an organisation is made by the analyst. A defensible assessment gives a graded claim, separates the distinctive observations from the common ones, and says what would move it.
questions.hint: Ask what else would produce that observation, and ask whether the claim is about a group or an operation.
questions.learningObjective: explain why attribution cannot reach certainty and what a good assessment says instead

answer.exemplar: The reason is a mismatch between the unit the limit is stated in and the unit the attacker is optimising, and the mismatch is structural rather than a matter of choosing the wrong number. A limit is always a statement about something countable: bytes in one request, records in one export, attempts from one address, connections in one minute. An adversary who wants to move a large quantity through a small limit does not need to defeat the counting; they need to spread the same quantity across enough separate instances that each one is under the threshold. The arithmetic is unfavourable in exactly the way that matters, because the cost to the attacker of splitting is a fixed overhead per instance while the benefit is that the limit is never approached, so the defence has to become more expensive exactly when the attacker is willing to spend more. Nothing about the threshold needs to be lowered to fix this, because lowering it punishes the wrong party: legitimate activity is the bulk of the traffic and it is not the party making the many small requests. The limit therefore has to be restated against a different subject. A threshold that is per account, or per process, or per destination, over a window, counts what the adversary is actually spending, and a small number of very large events then shows up as an aggregate even when each event is legal. The general form is worth stating because it applies well beyond security controls: any limit expressed per event is a limit an adversary can satisfy by using more events, so the question to ask of every threshold is what the thing being counted is, and whether the party being limited is the party doing the counting. Where a per-event limit has to be kept, because the cost of a per-subject account is unacceptable, the compensation is correlation: a rule that flags not one large event but many small ones in a period is the same protection stated in a form the adversary cannot satisfy by splitting.

questions.explanation: A per-event limit counts something the adversary can divide, and splitting is cheap to them and punishing to the limit. The limit has to be restated per subject over a window, or replaced by a rule that flags many small events in a period.
questions.hint: Ask what the limit counts, and which party is doing the counting.
questions.learningObjective: explain why per-event thresholds fail and what a threshold must be applied to

answer.exemplar: The technique is usually described as persuading the target to visit somewhere, and that description undersells it, because the target has already decided to visit and the attacker only has to change what is there. Two separate decisions were made earlier, without the attacker, and both still stand. The first is the network's: a destination was permitted, usually because the address was added to an allowance years ago for an ordinary reason, and a request to it is not unusual, does not breach a policy, and is not something a person notices. The second is the browser's: this origin is one the user has visited many times, so content from it is not treated as suspicious, and the origin is a legitimate place for code to run. The attacker in that position therefore holds two allowances that were granted for unrelated purposes, and neither has to be broken, forged, or escalated. That is why the position is valuable out of proportion to its apparent simplicity, and it is why the mitigations that matter are the ones that would have changed one of those decisions in advance: which destinations are permitted, and which origins may execute what. There is a third thing that is easy to add to the list and should be kept separate, because it is a consequence rather than a permission. Whatever the script does is constrained by what the browser will let an ordinary page do, and the site's own protections about framing and about what its content may reach shape what the attacker can use it for. Getting these three confused leads to bad controls: a defence aimed at blocking the site is fighting the last of them, and a defence aimed at the script's requests is aimed at the wrong layer entirely. The general shape is worth carrying to other problems: an attacker prefers to inherit a decision rather than to influence it, and the most useful control is the one that would have made the inherited decision the wrong one.

questions.explanation: The position inherits two prior decisions: the network already permits the destination and the browser already trusts the origin. Neither has to be broken, so controls aimed at blocking the site are fighting the wrong layer.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions were already made about that destination, and by whom.
questions.learningObjective: explain what an attacker gains from a position on a site the target already uses

answer.exemplar: A false positive in this setting is not an error in the abstract; it is a specific piece of an analyst's or an engineer's afternoon, and the cost is easy to state and routinely left out of the comparison. Somebody reads the alert, forms a view about how it got there, checks whether the host has a reason to be talking to that destination, checks whether the process is expected, and either closes it or opens an investigation. When the alert is a bad indicator, all of that work has produced nothing, and the important part is what happens the next time. An alert stream with a poor signal ratio does not merely consume time; it trains people to dismiss alerts, and the dismissal generalises. Once an analyst has learned that this class of alert is usually noise, the next alert in that class is closed without the checks, and the one that was real is closed with it. That is the cost that is not counted, and it is not proportional to the number of false positives; it is a property of the ratio, and it is why a feed that produces a great many matches is worse than no feed even when every match it produces is a true statement about something. The second cost, which is also unpriced, is the opportunity cost of the effort that went into processing them: a small team with a fixed number of hours spent on a feed is not spending them on the detections that would have found the thing. This is why the evaluation of a feed should be in the terms of a ratio and an expiry rather than a count of indicators, and why the number of indicators is close to meaningless as a measure of quality. A feed that carries a small number of well-dated, well-sourced indicators is more useful than one carrying a large catalogue of unexpired statements about activity that finished long ago, and the difference is not in the volume but in whether a match means anything when it arrives.

questions.explanation: A bad indicator costs an investigation that produces nothing, and worse, it teaches people to dismiss that class of alert, which then hides the real one. The cost is a property of the signal ratio, so feeds should be judged on that and on expiry, not on how many indicators they carry.
questions.hint: Ask what a responder does with each alert, and what they do differently after ten of them.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a false positive in a feed has a cost that is usually not counted

questions.explanation: From 01:05 to 01:52 is forty-seven minutes, and the number is worth computing rather than feeling because it is the pair of figures that get argued about: how long the party had before anybody knew, and how long the data was moving before the alert existed at all. The reconstruction gives different and more useful figures from the other anchors in the same window, and each of them belongs to a different owner. The interval from the staging of the archive to the first transfer measures how long the material sat before it moved. The interval from the alert to the credential or session being withdrawn measures the response. And the total from staging to the response measures the incident, which is the number a review will quote. The arithmetic also exposes something that is not arithmetic, and it is the point of doing it: a gap in one source in the middle of a window is ambiguous, because it can mean nothing happened or it can mean the feed stopped, and only the second is visible from the logs. So a timeline assembled from several sources needs its gaps stated rather than smoothed over, and a figure quoted as forty-seven minutes is only as good as the coverage between the two points.
questions.hint: Convert both times to minutes past midnight and subtract.
questions.learningObjective: compute a detection lag from two points on a timeline

questions.explanation: Four hundred thousand events a day at 0.05 per cent is two hundred matches a day, and the reason the number matters is not the arithmetic but what it implies about the ratio rather than the volume. Two hundred is not an alert load anybody can work through, so the practical consequence is not that two hundred investigations will happen but that a threshold will be applied somewhere, and the threshold is where the interesting decisions get made. Which events are checked first, whether a match on a short-lived indicator is treated differently from one on a current one, and whether a host that matches once in a month is escalated or recorded, are all decisions that a volume figure forces and that no rule makes for you. The same calculation in the other direction is the useful one, because it is the design target: two hundred a day is what a ratio of one in two thousand buys, and a rule that produced ten would need a ratio of one in forty thousand, which is a different and much more selective feed. So the number is a starting point for asking whether the feed's claim about its own quality survives contact with the estate it is being connected to, since the same feed is more or less useful against a large estate than a small one. The common mistake is to quote the number of indicators the feed carries, which is a different quantity entirely and says nothing about how often anything will match.
questions.hint: Multiply the daily count by the percentage expressed as a fraction.
questions.learningObjective: compute a daily false-positive load from a feed rate
